title: Fall Asleep Fast 🌙 6 Gentle Stories Under the Stars | Snortlo
intro: Hello, and welcome. This is Snortlo, and tonight I have six gentle stories for you, about a rainy tea shop, a quiet museum, a sleepy orchard, and a few warm places in between. Before we begin, let yourself get comfortable. Dim the lights, or turn them off. Let the pillow take the weight of your head, and let your hands rest wherever they like. You don't need to stay awake until the end. If you drift off along the way, that is just fine. The stories will carry on softly without you. Let's take one slow breath together. In, and out. Good. Let's begin.

stories.title: The Tea Shop on a Rainy Afternoon
stories.text:
On the corner of a narrow street in a small market town, there was a tea shop with a green door and a bell that went ting when you opened it. Inside there were six little tables, a long wooden counter, and three tidy shelves of tea tins, each one with a handwritten label.

The shop belonged to a woman called Nora. She wore a blue apron with a pencil in the pocket that she almost never used. Nora did not need to write things down. She remembered.

On this particular afternoon, it was raining. It was a steady, patient rain that sounded like it planned to stay all day. It pattered on the awning and ran down the front window in little wandering lines. The street outside turned shiny and grey, and umbrellas bobbed past.

Inside, it was warm. The big kettle hummed to itself, and the lamps were already on, though it was only half past two, because rainy afternoons always feel a little later than they are. Then the bell went ting.

It was Mr. Pell. He was a tall, thin man with a wet hat and a newspaper under his arm, and he always sat at the table by the radiator.

"Afternoon, Nora," he said, shaking the rain off his hat.

"Afternoon, Mr. Pell," said Nora. She was already reaching for the tin with the dark red label. Strong black tea, brewed for four minutes, not three and not five, with a splash of milk and two sugars. She did not ask. She never asked. Mr. Pell sat down, unfolded his newspaper, and by the time he had found the page he liked, his tea was beside him, steaming.

"Perfect," he said, without looking up. He said that every day too.

The bell went ting again. In came Mrs. Lowe, who was small and round and wore a bright yellow raincoat that squeaked a little when she moved. She had a shopping bag in each hand.

"Oh, it's wet out there," she said. "It's ever so wet."

"It is," said Nora kindly. "Sit down and warm up."

Mrs. Lowe liked lemon and ginger, in the tall glass cup with the little handle, and one of the oat biscuits from the jar at the end of the counter. Nora brought them over on a small plate with a paper napkin folded into a triangle. Mrs. Lowe let out a long, happy sigh and wrapped both hands around the glass.

For a while, nobody came in. Mr. Pell turned a page. Mrs. Lowe dipped her biscuit in her tea. Nora watched the raindrops race each other down the window. She always picked one and hoped it would win. It usually didn't, but she didn't mind.

Ting. The bell again.

This time it was June, the schoolteacher, with a bag of exercise books and a pair of spectacles that steamed up the moment she stepped into the warm.

"I can't see a thing," she laughed, taking them off and wiping them on her scarf.

"Peppermint?" said Nora.

"Peppermint," said June. "With honey. You know me too well."

June liked the cup with the blue flowers on it. She sat in the corner with her red pen and began to mark, and every so often she smiled at something a child had written.

Then came Theo. Theo was young and cheerful, with rain dripping off the end of his nose. He worked at the hardware shop two doors down.

"Today," he announced, standing at the counter and looking up at all the tins, "I'm going to try something new."

"Are you?" said Nora.

"I am. Something adventurous." He read the labels very seriously, one by one. Jasmine. Smoky black. Chamomile. Rose and vanilla.

Nora waited. She had already taken down the cocoa tin.

"Actually," said Theo, "I'll have a hot chocolate, please."

"With the little marshmallows?"

"With the little marshmallows," he agreed, a bit sheepishly. "I'll be adventurous tomorrow."

"Tomorrow's a good day for it," said Nora, and she made his hot chocolate with exactly seven little marshmallows on top, because that was how many fitted without any falling off.

The afternoon went on in its slow, rainy way. A father and his small daughter shared a slice of lemon cake and both got icing on their noses. An old man liked his tea so weak it was almost warm water, and told Nora it was the best cup in town. Nora remembered each of them, who liked the window and who liked the corner, who wanted the big cup and who wanted the little one.

Then, a little before four, the bell went ting and a woman came in whom Nora had never seen before. She was wet through, and she stood just inside the door looking a little lost.

"Come in," said Nora. "Come and get warm."

The woman sat down near the counter and looked up at all the tins.

"I'm not sure what I want," she said. "Something warm. Something that tastes like being at home."

Nora looked at the woman's tired eyes and the way she sat with her shoulders up near her ears. Then she took down a tin from the end of the second shelf, a soft, malty tea with a little cinnamon in it. She poured it into a plain white cup with a splash of warm milk.

The woman took a sip. Her shoulders came down, slowly, all the way.

"Oh," she said quietly. "That's it. That's exactly it."

Nora smiled and made a little note in her head, beside all the other little notes. Malty tea, cinnamon, warm milk. Next time, she would remember.

By five o'clock, the street lamps were on, and the rain under them looked like falling silver thread. One by one, the customers put on their coats. Mr. Pell tipped his hat. Mrs. Lowe squeaked out into the evening. June packed away her books, full of little ticks and stars. The woman in the wet coat was the last to leave.

"Thank you," she said at the door. "I'll come back."

"I'll be here," said Nora.

Ting went the bell, and then the shop was quiet.

Nora turned the little sign in the window so it said closed. She washed the cups in warm soapy water and dried them, and put the blue flowered cup back in its place, and the tall glass cup, and the plain white one. She swept the floor, and the broom went shh, shh, shh across the boards.

Then she made herself a cup of tea. Just a simple one, nothing fancy, with a little milk. She sat at the table by the window and held it in both hands and listened.

The rain was still falling. It pattered on the awning. It ran down the glass in slow, wandering lines. The radiator ticked. The big kettle, cooling now, gave one last little sigh.

Nora finished her tea. She switched off the lamps, one by one, until only the small light above the counter was left glowing. She buttoned her coat and stepped outside and locked the green door behind her.

And the tea shop sat quietly on its corner, warm and dark, with all its tins asleep on their shelves, listening to the rain.

stories.title: The Lambing Shed
stories.text:
At the bottom of a long, muddy lane, on a small farm with a crooked gate and a red front door, there was a wooden shed with a tin roof. In the spring, the shed was where the new lambs slept. And in the spring, at night, the shed was where Walt worked.

Walt was the night nurse for the lambs. He was not a young man anymore. He had a grey beard, a woolly hat, and very large boots. In the daytime, his niece Ruth ran the farm. But at night, Walt took over. He liked it that way. He said lambs were good company, and they never asked him to fix the tractor.

On this particular night, it was clear and still. A thin moon hung over the hill, and the grass in the top field was silver with dew. Walt pulled on his boots, buttoned his old wax jacket, and picked up the wicker basket from the kitchen table. In the basket were four glass bottles of warm milk, each one wrapped in a tea towel to keep it cosy, and a flask of tea for himself.

"Off you go, then," said Ruth from the stairs, in her dressing gown.

"Off I go," said Walt.

He walked down the lane with his torch making a little round puddle of light in front of him. The mud went squelch, squelch under his boots. The farm dog, Bramble, lifted her head from her bed in the porch, decided it was only Walt, and put it down again.

Inside the shed, it smelled of clean straw and warm wool and something milky and sweet. There was one lamp hanging from a hook in the middle of the roof, and when Walt switched it on it gave a soft yellow glow, just enough to see by and not so much that anyone would be startled.

Along one wall there were little pens made of wooden hurdles, each one bedded deep with golden straw. And in the pens were the lambs.

There were four of them who needed bottles tonight, the small ones who needed a little extra. Their mothers were nearby, in the big pen at the end. Walt had given them names that were not very imaginative, but which suited them.

There was Pip, who was the smallest, with a white face and one black ear. There was Dot, who had a dark spot on her nose. There was Clover, who was always asleep. And there was Bertie, who was always awake, and who always wanted to be first.

"Evening, all," said Walt softly.

Bertie stood up at once and said, "Meh," in a high, wobbly voice. Pip stood up too, though more slowly, and stretched one back leg out behind him, then the other. Dot blinked. Clover did not move at all.

Walt climbed over the low hurdle and sat down on the upturned bucket he kept in the corner. He took the first bottle out of the basket, unwrapped it, and tested a drop on the inside of his wrist. Warm, but not hot. Just right.

Bertie came at once, of course. He wagged his tail so fast it was almost a blur, and drank with tremendous energy, pushing with his head every few seconds, as if the bottle might be hiding more milk somewhere at the back.

"Steady," said Walt. "There's no rush. Nobody's going to take it."

Bertie did not believe him, and drank the whole bottle in about a minute. Then he stood there with milk on his chin, looking enormously pleased with himself, and wobbled off to lie down in the straw.

Next was Pip. Pip was slower and more careful. He sniffed the bottle first, as if checking it was the same bottle as last night. Then he drank in little gulps, stopping now and then to look up at Walt with his round dark eyes. Walt didn't hurry him. He hummed an old tune, very low, with no words. The lamp swung a tiny bit on its hook. The tin roof made a soft tick as the night grew colder.

When Pip had finished, Walt rubbed him gently behind his black ear, and Pip leaned into his hand and closed his eyes.

Dot was next. Dot was polite about it. She drank steadily, with her spotted nose wrinkling, and when she was done she gave a small, satisfied, "Meh," as if to say thank you, that was very nice.

That left Clover.

Clover was still asleep, curled into a tight woolly ball in the corner of the pen with her nose tucked under her own back leg. Walt looked at her for a moment and smiled.

"Clover," he said. "Supper time."

Nothing.

"Clover."

One ear twitched.

Walt picked her up very gently and set her on his lap, where she lay like a warm loaf of bread. He held the bottle near her nose. She sniffed, still with her eyes shut. Then, very slowly, she began to drink. She drank the whole bottle without once opening her eyes. When it was empty she gave a tiny sigh, rested her chin on Walt's arm, and went straight back to sleep.

"Well," said Walt. "That's one way to do it."

He sat for a while with Clover on his lap. It was very quiet in the shed. One of the mothers in the big pen shifted in the straw and gave a low, deep, "Baa," the kind that just means, I'm here. A lamb answered her from somewhere in the dark. Then quiet again.

Walt poured himself a cup of tea from the flask. Steam curled up in the lamplight. He drank it slowly, with his free hand, while Clover breathed in and out against his arm.

Outside, the moon moved a little further across the sky. The wind came up for a moment and made the tin roof creak, then went away again.

When his tea was finished, Walt laid Clover down in the straw beside Dot, who shuffled over to make room. Pip had already curled up against Bertie, and Bertie, for once, was asleep. Four small woolly shapes in a row, rising and falling.

Walt checked the water buckets. He fluffed up the straw in the corner where it had gone flat. He walked along the pens and looked at each of the mothers and each of the lambs, and they looked back at him, sleepy and calm. Everything was as it should be.

He would come back again in a few hours, before the sun came up, with four more bottles. But for now, there was nothing more to do.

He put the empty bottles in the basket and folded the tea towels over them. He stood in the doorway for a moment, looking back at the golden straw and the soft lamplight and the little sleeping lambs.

"Goodnight, all," he whispered.

Then he switched off the lamp. The shed went dark and warm and still. He lifted the latch, and pushed, and closed the door behind him.

Walt walked back up the lane under the thin moon, with his torch making its little round puddle of light. Squelch, squelch went the mud. In the porch, Bramble thumped her tail once on her bed.

And down in the shed, in the straw, the lambs slept on, breathing softly in the dark. In, and out. In, and out.

stories.title: The Night Watchman
stories.text:
In the middle of a quiet town, between the library and a little park with a fountain, there was a small museum. It had stone steps, two tall wooden doors, and a brass plaque by the entrance that had been polished so often the letters had gone soft at the edges. It was not a famous museum. It had a room of old maps, a room of pottery, a room of stuffed birds in glass cases, and, up the wide staircase, a long gallery of paintings.

Every night, when the visitors had gone home and the doors were locked, Henry came on duty.

Henry was the night watchman. He had a dark blue jacket with silver buttons, a cap he wore slightly to one side, and a torch that he hardly ever needed. In all his years at the museum, nothing very much had happened. That was exactly how he liked it.

On this particular evening, he arrived at seven, just as the day staff were leaving. Miss Fern from the front desk waved to him as she buttoned her coat.

"All quiet," she said. "A school trip this morning. Somebody left a mitten in the bird room."

"I'll keep an eye on it," said Henry.

When everyone had gone, he locked the big doors behind them. The sound echoed softly through the building, a deep wooden thunk. Then the museum was his.

Henry liked to start with a cup of tea. He made it in the little staff kitchen behind the gift shop, in a mug with a picture of a lighthouse on it, and he drank it standing by the window, looking out at the park. The fountain had been turned off for the night, and the lamps along the path glowed orange.

Then Henry began his round.

He always went the same way. First the map room, where the old maps hung in their frames, showing coastlines and rivers and little drawings of ships and sea creatures in the corners. He walked slowly past each one, shining his torch on the floor, not on the maps, because the maps didn't like bright light.

"Goodnight, maps," he said.

Next was the pottery room. Bowls and jugs and plates sat on their shelves behind the glass, some of them painted with flowers, some plain and brown and simple. One jug had a small chip in its spout. Henry always thought it looked a bit embarrassed about it.

"Goodnight, pottery," he said. "Don't worry about the chip. Nobody minds."

Then the bird room. The birds stood very still in their cases, as they always did, with their glass eyes catching the light from the corridor. There was a heron on one leg, a pair of robins on a branch, a barn owl with its wings half open. On the bench in the middle of the room, just as Miss Fern had said, there was a small red mitten.

Henry picked it up. It was soft and woolly and had a snowflake knitted on the back. He took it down to the front desk and put it in the lost property box, on top of an umbrella, a scarf, and a single grey glove that had been waiting for its owner since the spring.

"There," he said. "Now you've got company."

Then he climbed the wide staircase. Each step creaked in its own particular way, and Henry knew them all. The third step went eek. The seventh step went ork. The top step said nothing at all, which Henry thought was very dignified of it.

At the top was the long gallery.

This was Henry's favourite part. The gallery was long and narrow, with a polished wooden floor and a row of tall windows down one side. On the other wall hung the paintings, each one with its own small lamp above it. At night, Henry switched the little lamps down low, so the paintings glowed softly, like windows into other places.

He walked down the gallery very slowly, and stopped in front of each one.

The first painting was of a harbour at sunset, with fishing boats tied up at the quay and gulls sitting on the posts. The water was pink and gold.

"Goodnight, harbour," said Henry. "Goodnight, boats."

The next was a portrait of a woman in a green dress, sitting very straight in a chair, with a small brown dog on her lap. The woman looked rather serious. The dog looked as though it was thinking about biscuits.

"Goodnight, madam," said Henry, and gave a little nod. "Goodnight, dog."

Then came a painting of a snowy village, with smoke curling up from the chimneys and a single lit window in a cottage at the end of the lane. Henry always lingered at this one. He liked to imagine who lived in the cottage, and what they were having for supper. Tonight, he decided, it was soup. Leek and potato, with thick bread.

"Goodnight, village," he said.

There was a painting of a bowl of pears on a blue cloth, which he wished goodnight to as well, because it seemed rude not to. There was a painting of a field of sheep under a wide grey sky. There was a little one, no bigger than a book, of a cat asleep on a windowsill in the sun. Henry liked the cat very much. It had the look of someone who had never once been in a hurry.

"Goodnight, cat," he said softly. "Sleep well. Not that you need telling."

At the very end of the gallery was the biggest painting of all. It showed a wide calm lake at evening, with mountains behind it and a single rowing boat pulled up on the shore. The sky was turning from blue to violet, and one small star had come out above the mountains.

Henry stood in front of it for a long time. Then he took off his cap and held it in his hands.

"Goodnight, lake," he said. "Goodnight, everyone."

The gallery was very quiet. Through the tall windows, the moon had risen over the park. Its light fell in long pale squares across the floor. Henry could hear the old building settling around him, the small creaks and ticks of wood and pipes, the faint hum of the lamps. Somewhere downstairs, a clock struck ten, slowly. Dong. Dong. Dong.

He went back down the creaking stairs, eek, ork, and nothing. He checked the doors and the windows. He checked the back door by the kitchen and the little side door by the gift shop. Everything was locked and still.

Then he made a second cup of tea in the lighthouse mug and took it to his chair at the front desk. It was an old leather chair with a dip in the seat exactly the shape of Henry. He sat down, put his cap on the desk, and opened his book. It was a long, slow novel in which nothing much happened, which was why he liked it.

Every hour he would get up and walk the round again. The maps, the pottery, the birds, the stairs, the gallery. But for now, he sat and read, and sipped his tea, while the museum slept around him.

The lamps in the gallery glowed softly above the paintings. The harbour, the village, the cat on the windowsill, the lake with its single star. All of them quiet. All of them safe.

Henry turned a page. The clock ticked. And outside, in the park, the moon went on shining on the still fountain.

stories.title: Mending the Nets
stories.text:
In a small fishing town, where the houses sat close together on the side of a hill and all their windows looked out to sea, there was a cottage at the very end of the harbour wall. It had white walls, a blue door, and a lamp in the front window that was lit every evening when the boats were out.

The cottage belonged to June. Her husband, Tom, was a fisherman, and on evenings when the boats were out, June mended the nets.

She did it at the kitchen table, under the lamp, with the window open just a crack so she could hear the sea. The nets came in great soft heaps of brown and green, smelling of salt and seaweed and rope. Here and there were holes, some small, some big enough to put your hand through. June found every one of them.

On this particular evening, the weather was calm. The sun had gone down behind the headland, and the sky over the water was fading to a deep, soft blue. Small waves came in against the harbour wall, one after another, with a gentle hush.

June put the kettle on. She lit the lamp in the window and turned the wick up until the flame was steady and bright. Then she sat down at the table, pulled the first net onto her lap, and picked up her netting needle.

The needle was made of smooth pale wood, long and flat, with twine wound around it. It had belonged to her grandmother. It fitted her hand exactly, as if it had been waiting for her.

She found the first hole quickly. It was near the edge, where the net must have caught on a rock. June looked at it for a moment, the way you look at a crossword clue, and then she began. Under, over, through, and pull. Under, over, through, and pull. Each little square of the net took shape again, knot by knot, until the hole was gone and you could hardly tell it had ever been there.

The kettle began to sing. June got up and made her tea in the big brown pot and poured it into her favourite mug, the one with a crack in the handle that she had glued herself. She put it on the windowsill next to the lamp.

Then she looked out at the sea.

Far out, beyond the harbour wall, there were small lights on the water. They were the boats. From here, they looked no bigger than fireflies.

June went back to her net. Under, over, through, and pull.

Her cat, Moss, came in from the hall and jumped up onto the chair beside her. Moss was a large grey cat with a white chest, and she was very interested in nets. She liked to pat the loose ends of twine with one paw, very gently, as if she were helping.

"Thank you, Moss," said June. "That's very useful."

Moss blinked at her, then curled up on the chair with her tail over her nose and watched the needle go in and out.

The clock on the mantelpiece ticked. The lamp flame stood still and steady. Outside, the waves said hush, hush against the stones.

After a while, June heard a low, steady sound from the harbour. Put, put, put, put. It was an engine. She looked up and saw the first boat coming in past the end of the wall, its lights swaying gently. It was the little green boat that belonged to old Mr. Finch. He always came in first. He said it was because he was the best fisherman in town. Everyone else said it was because he liked his supper.

The boat bumped softly against the quay, and Mr. Finch climbed out, slow and careful, and tied his rope to the iron ring. He looked up at her window and raised one hand. June raised hers back.

Then she bent over the net again. Under, over, through, and pull.

The second boat came in a little while later. It was the red one, belonging to the Hale brothers, who were very large and very quiet and who always seemed to be eating a sandwich. One of the brothers waved at June's window. She waved back.

The tea in her mug was half gone now. The sky had turned dark blue, then darker still, and the first stars had come out over the headland. The harbour lamps were lit along the quay, and their light shimmered on the water in long wobbly stripes.

June finished the net on her lap and folded it carefully, the way her grandmother had shown her. The next one had only one small hole, and she mended it in no time at all.

A third boat came in. Then a fourth. Each time, June heard the engine first, put, put, put, put, then saw the lights swing around the end of the wall, then heard the bump and the rope and the boots. Each time, someone looked up at her lamp in the window and lifted a hand. That was what the lamp was for, really. Not for the boats to find their way. They knew their way. It was just so that everyone coming home could see that someone was there.

Moss had fallen asleep. Her side went up and down very slowly.

By now there was only one light left out on the water. June knew which one it was. It was a small blue boat with a white stripe, and it was called the Rosie, after Tom's mother. It was always the last one in, because Tom always went the furthest, and always took his time.

June put down her needle. She took her mug from the windowsill, found that it had gone cold, and made a fresh pot. She warmed a second mug, too, and put it ready on the table.

Then she sat by the window and watched the little light come closer.

It came slowly across the dark, flat sea. Then she heard it. Put, put, put, put. Then the lights swung round the end of the harbour wall, and there was the Rosie, blue and white, sliding in under the harbour lamps.

June watched Tom tie the boat up. She watched him lift out his boxes and stack them neatly on the quay. She watched him stand for a moment, stretching his back, and then look up toward the cottage at the end of the wall.

He raised his hand.

June raised hers.

She poured his tea, with milk and one sugar. She folded the last net and put it on top of the pile. She tucked her grandmother's needle into the drawer of the kitchen table, where it lived.

Then she went to the window and turned the lamp down, lower and lower, until the flame was just a small, soft glow. All the boats were home.

Outside, the harbour was still. The boats sat side by side along the quay, rocking very gently on the tide. The water lapped against their wooden sides. Hush, hush, hush.

The blue door opened, and Tom came in, bringing the cool sea air with him.

"Evening," he said.

"Evening," said June. "Your tea's ready."

And in the window, the little lamp glowed softly over the quiet harbour, until it was time for bed.

stories.title: The Owl in the Orchard
stories.text:
At the edge of a small village, behind a low stone wall, there was an old apple orchard. It had seven long rows of trees, a wooden gate that was usually left open, and a little stream running along the bottom where the grass grew long and soft. In the daytime, people came to sit in the shade, or to pick apples, or to let their children run up and down between the rows. But at night, the orchard belonged to the owl.

The owl lived in the oldest tree of all, a wide twisted apple tree at the very top of the orchard, with a hollow in its trunk just the right size for an owl. She had lived there for a long time. She had soft brown feathers, a pale round face, and two large dark eyes that saw everything. And she approved of very little.

Every evening, as the sun went down and the sky turned the colour of apricots, she came out of her hollow, shook out her feathers, and settled on her favourite branch. From there, she could see the whole orchard. It was her job, she felt, to keep watch over it while it slept.

On this particular evening, it was early autumn. The air was cool and smelled of ripe apples and damp grass. The last of the light was fading behind the hill, and a few early stars were coming out.

The owl looked down at the orchard. She sighed.

"Well," she said to herself. "Let's see what's what."

First, she looked at the apples. The trees were heavy with them, red and gold and green, hanging in clusters among the leaves. Several had fallen into the grass. The owl did not approve of this. Apples, in her opinion, should stay where they were put.

"Untidy," she murmured.

Then she looked at the bench by the gate. Someone had left a cardigan on it, a blue one, folded over the back. The owl did not approve of this either. Benches were for sitting, not for leaving things.

"Careless," she said.

A small hedgehog came trundling out from under the hedge. It snuffled along the bottom row of trees, found a fallen apple, and began to eat it with loud, wet, crunching noises.

The owl watched it for a long moment.

"Noisy," she said.

The hedgehog did not hear her, or if it did, it did not care. It went on crunching.

The sky grew darker. The stars came out properly now, more and more of them, until the whole sky was speckled. A thin breeze moved through the orchard, and the leaves whispered against each other. Somewhere down by the stream, a frog said something low and gravelly, and another frog answered.

The owl turned her head all the way round to look at the stream, then all the way back again.

"Frogs," she said. "Always talking. Never saying anything."

A family of rabbits came out from the long grass at the bottom of the orchard. There were five of them, a mother and four young ones, and they hopped about in the moonlight, nibbling the clover and chasing each other in small circles. One of the young ones tried to jump over a fallen apple, misjudged it, and landed on its nose. It sat up, looking surprised, and then went on as though nothing had happened.

The owl watched this very closely.

"Undignified," she said. But she said it a little more softly than before.

The moon rose over the hill, round and white and very bright. It lit up the whole orchard. Every tree had a long shadow, and every apple had a little silver shine on it. The stream glittered at the bottom of the field.

The owl fluffed up her feathers against the cool air and settled more comfortably on her branch.

A little later, a fox came through the gate. It was a young fox, thin and red, with a white tip to its tail. It walked along the rows with its nose to the ground, very carefully, as if it were looking for something it had dropped. It found the blue cardigan on the bench, sniffed it all over, and then lay down on it, curled up in a tight ball, with its tail over its face.

The owl stared at the fox for a very long time.

"Well," she said at last. "At least someone is using it."

The night went on. The owl kept watch. She watched the hedgehog finish its apple and trundle off to find another. She watched the rabbits go back into the long grass, one by one, the smallest last. She watched a moth flutter round and round the top of the gatepost, then drift away into the dark. She listened to the frogs, and the stream, and the leaves, and the very faint sound of the fox breathing in its sleep.

At some point, very late, a light came on in the farmhouse across the field. It was a small yellow square in the darkness. The owl watched it. After a while, it went out again.

"Good," she said. "About time."

Then, just for a moment, the whole orchard went completely still. The breeze stopped. The frogs stopped. The leaves stopped whispering. It was so quiet the owl could hear an apple, somewhere at the far end of the third row, come loose from its stem and fall, very softly, into the grass. Thup.

The owl looked at the orchard spread out below her in the moonlight. The seven long rows of trees, heavy with fruit. The silver grass. The stream. The bench by the gate with a fox asleep on it. The hedgehog snuffling in the hedge. The dark place in the long grass where the rabbits were sleeping, all five of them, in a warm heap.

She looked at all of it, and she did not say anything for a while.

Then she said, very quietly, "It will do."

Which, for an owl who approved of very little, was the highest praise there was.

The night went on, slow and calm. The moon crossed the sky and began to sink toward the trees on the other side of the valley. The stars turned. The air grew colder, and a thin mist rose from the stream and drifted up between the rows, soft and white, curling round the trunks of the trees.

The owl stayed on her branch. She kept her watch. Every now and then she turned her head one way, then the other, just to be sure. Everything was where it ought to be. Or near enough.

And when, at last, the sky in the east began to turn pale, she gave one long, low call across the orchard. Hoo. Hooo. It meant that the night was over, and that everything had been looked after.

Then she ruffled her feathers, stepped back into her hollow in the old apple tree, tucked her head down into her soft brown chest, and closed her large dark eyes.

Below her, the orchard slept on, quiet and misty and full of apples, waiting for the morning.

stories.title: Stars from the Roof
stories.text:
On a quiet street at the top of a small town, there was a tall, narrow house with a crooked chimney and a flat bit of roof at the back. You could get to the flat bit through a little window at the top of the stairs, if you were careful, and if you had permission. Mabel had permission, as long as her grandfather came too.

Her grandfather was called Arthur. He had white hair that stuck up at the back, a thick green jumper with leather patches on the elbows, and a telescope that was older than anyone could remember. It was made of brass, with a long wooden case lined with faded red velvet, and it lived on top of the wardrobe in the spare room. On clear nights, it came down.

On this particular night, the sky was perfectly clear.

Mabel had been watching it all evening, through the kitchen window while they ate their supper. At first it was pale blue, then a deeper blue, then a soft, velvety dark. And now, at last, the first stars were coming out.

"Grandad," said Mabel. "It's time."

Her grandfather looked up from his armchair, where he had been pretending to read the paper.

"Is it?" he said. "Are you sure?"

"It's definitely time."

"Well then," he said, folding the paper. "We'd better get ready."

Getting ready took a while, and that was part of it. First, Mabel put on her pyjamas, her thick socks, her dressing gown, her woolly hat, and her big coat on top of everything, so she looked like a small round bundle with a face. Then her grandfather made cocoa. He made it in a pan on the stove, the proper way, stirring slowly with a wooden spoon. He poured it into a tall tartan flask and screwed the lid on tight.

Then he took down two blankets from the cupboard, two cushions from the sofa, and the telescope from the top of the wardrobe.

They climbed the stairs together. The flask clinked against the telescope case. At the top, her grandfather opened the little window, and a breath of cool night air came in, smelling of chimney smoke and autumn leaves. He climbed out first, slowly, and then helped Mabel through after him.

The flat bit of roof was just big enough for two people, two cushions, and one telescope. There was a low wall around the edge, and from there you could see right across the town. All the rooftops and chimneys. The clock tower. The park, dark and still. The streetlights in long, curving rows, and here and there a lit window, yellow and warm.

But mostly, you could see the sky.

They put the cushions down and wrapped themselves in the blankets. Her grandfather opened the wooden case, and Mabel helped him lift the telescope out and set it up on its three thin legs. It squeaked a little, as it always did.

"Right," he said. "Cocoa first, or stars first?"

Mabel thought about this very seriously.

"Cocoa first," she said. "Then stars."

He unscrewed the flask and poured the cocoa into the two little cups that fitted on top. Steam rose up into the cold air and vanished. Mabel held her cup in both hands, mittens and all, and sipped. It was hot and sweet and tasted like the best thing in the world.

They sat side by side and drank their cocoa and looked up.

The stars were coming out properly now, more and more of them, as if someone were sprinkling them across the sky a handful at a time. Some were bright and steady. Some were small and faint and twinkled when you looked straight at them, and seemed to disappear, then came back when you looked a little to the side.

"Why do they do that?" asked Mabel.

"Shy, I expect," said her grandfather. "Some of them don't like being stared at."

When the cocoa was finished, it was time for the telescope.

Her grandfather bent down and looked through the little eyepiece, and turned the brass knob very slowly, and moved the telescope a tiny bit to the left, and then a tiny bit back. He was humming to himself, the way he always did when he was concentrating.

"There," he said at last. "Have a look."

Mabel put her eye to the eyepiece. At first, all she could see was black. Then she held very still, and there it was. The moon. Not the whole moon, just a part of it, but enormous and bright and silvery grey, covered in craters and soft shadows and long pale lines, like a very old plate that had been dropped and mended.

"Oh," said Mabel. She didn't say anything else for quite a long time.

After the moon, they looked at a bright star that wasn't really a star, but a planet. Through the telescope it was a tiny round disc, creamy yellow, with four little dots of light lined up beside it.

"Those are its moons," said her grandfather.

"It has four moons?"

"At least four. Those are the ones you can see from a roof."

Mabel thought it must be very nice to have four moons. It would never be properly dark.

Then they looked at a little fuzzy cluster of stars, all close together, like a handful of sugar spilled on a dark tablecloth. Her grandfather said they were called the Seven Sisters. Mabel counted them and only got to six, and her grandfather said that was perfectly normal, and that one of the sisters was probably having an early night.

After that, they didn't use the telescope very much. They lay back on the cushions with the blankets pulled up to their chins and looked at the sky with just their eyes. Her grandfather pointed out the shapes. The big saucepan. The lady sitting in her chair. The great hunter, just rising over the rooftops, with three bright stars in a row for his belt.

Mabel tried to keep her eyes open. The sky was so big, and so full, and so quiet. A soft breeze moved over the rooftops. Somewhere below, a cat walked along a garden wall. A car went by in the next street, very quietly, and then there was no sound at all.

"Grandad," said Mabel sleepily. "Will they still be there tomorrow?"

"Every one of them," said her grandfather. "They're very reliable. That's what I like about them."

Mabel's eyes closed. Then opened. Then closed again.

Her grandfather looked at her, all bundled up in her blanket and her woolly hat, breathing slow and deep. He smiled. He packed the telescope carefully back into its velvet case, and screwed the lid onto the empty flask, and folded his own blanket over his arm.

Then he lifted Mabel, blanket and all, and carried her back through the little window, and down the stairs, and into her bedroom. He took off her coat and her hat and tucked her into bed. She didn't wake up. She just sighed and turned over and pulled the covers up round her ears.

Her grandfather stood in the doorway for a moment. Through her window, he could see a little square of the night sky, with three or four stars in it.

"Goodnight, Mabel," he whispered.

He switched off the landing light. And outside, above the quiet town, the stars went on shining, every one of them, exactly where they were supposed to be.

outro: And that is the end of tonight's stories. Let everything go quiet now. The tea shop is sleeping on its corner in the rain, and the lambs are breathing softly in the straw. Henry is turning a page while the museum dreams, the lamp glows low over the harbour, the owl is tucked into her hollow, and Mabel is fast asleep beneath the stars. There are more stories waiting on the channel whenever you need them. Goodnight. Sleep well.
description:
Six cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly to help you rest and fall asleep.
A tea shop on a rainy afternoon, a lambing shed at night, a museum watchman, a harbour cottage where the nets are mended, an owl in an apple orchard, and a rooftop full of stars.
No cliffhangers, no drama. Just quiet places and kind hearts.
Goodnight 🌙
